claims.text: The component material is prone to hot cracking during high-temperature fusion-welding repair because of its microstructure.
Hot cracking during fusion-welding repair damages critical regions of the component.
A diffusion-based cladding process can deposit a compatible, high-melting-point alloy as a protective surface layer.
Laser-assisted coating deposition is an alternative process for applying the proposed repair layer.
The repaired component must tolerate high cyclic thermal loads.
The repaired component must tolerate mechanical stresses under aggressive operating conditions.
The proposed repair avoids the thermal cycles typical of conventional fusion welding.
Diffusion bonding at the coating-substrate interface can strengthen the bond between the coating and substrate.
A graded compositional transition at the coating-substrate interface reduces thermal-expansion misfit.
A graded coating-substrate interface reduces residual stresses.
The tailored cladding layer mitigates rapid heating and cooling relative to traditional fusion welding.
Mitigating rapid heating and cooling prevents hot-crack nucleation.
The proposed coating repair can avoid the hot-cracking problems associated with traditional fusion-welding repair.
The proposed coating repair allows the damaged component to remain in service under aggressive operating conditions without replacement of the entire part.
The coating-repaired component will have greater resistance to hot cracking than a traditionally fusion-welded repair.
The coating-repaired component will perform better under high cyclic thermal loads than a traditionally fusion-welded repair.
Traditional fusion-welding repair exposes the material to high thermal gradients.
Hot cracking caused by traditional fusion-welding repair compromises structural integrity.
The proposed intervention is expected to remain effective only when material, thermal-load, and mechanical-load conditions are comparable to the original service environment.

contradictions.description: The main hypothesis implies that the coating repair does not trigger hot cracking, whereas the predicted outcome and falsification rule require only a relative or statistically significant reduction in hot cracking, permitting residual cracking.
